title: Arrivée au Laser Game  (Arrival at the Laser Game)

segments.t: At the laser game arena, young guests eagerly await the guest of honor for Elvis's tenth birthday party. When internet star Norman Thavaud arrives, the excitement peaks as he meets the birthday boy and gets ready for battle. Listen to the scene in French first. Don't worry about catching every word.
Now let's break down the scene step by step. Listen to each line, followed by its meaning and a short explanation.
'Look, Norman is finally here!' Literally 'in end', that punchy two-syllable word tucked after 'is' means 'finally' or 'at last' in French.
'Hello to all the children!' Putting 'to' before 'all the children' turns a plain greeting into a stage-style shout-out to a crowd in French.
'Can I have an autograph?' Keeping 'I can have' in statement order with rising pitch is a polite, natural request for kids and adults alike in French.
'Yes of course, with pleasure.' Pairing 'well sure' with 'with pleasure' gives you a warm, reusable acceptance you can say in almost any situation.
'Who is the boss here?' Beyond restaurant kitchens, the term borrowed into English as 'chef' simply means 'leader' or 'boss' anywhere in French.
'I am the big boss!' Pointing to yourself in French uses 'it is me' up front rather than 'I am', giving Elvis's boast extra punch.
'You challenged me to the game?' Related to English 'defy', this action means 'challenged' in French, linking to 'the game' with 'at the'.
'Yes, I have a great team.' Casual 'super' never takes an ending before 'team', which shares a distant root with English 'equip' in French.
'I am very good too.' Literally 'very strong', that everyday compliment is how French speakers say someone is 'really skilled' at a game or subject.
'It is your birthday today, Elvis.' Even though 'birthday' starts with a vowel sound, 'your' already uses its '-on' form since 'birthday' is male-gendered in French.
'We are going to win the game!' Referring to a single round or match of laser tag, cards, or chess, French uses a word meaning 'part' rather than the general sport word.
'Do not be too shy.' Built on an irregular command stem of 'be', this gentle 'do not be' encouragement ends with a close cognate of 'timid' meaning 'shy'.
'Have good fun all together.' Literally 'amuse yourselves well', that cheerful send-off is what you'd say for 'have a great time!' to a group in French.

'Here we go for the fight!' Literally 'it is departed', this high-energy three-word idiom launches games, trips, and shows just like 'here we go!' in English. Now let's listen to the whole exchange once more from beginning to end.

Surrounded by cheering kids, Norman dives into the laser tag arena to give Elvis an unforgettable birthday match. Notice how French pairs going with a second action to talk confidently about what is about to happen. See you next time!

lines.fragment: Le gamin de 10 ans qui m'a défié au laser game ?
